summary: Recommend approve_with_caution. Evidence is solid: 55 tests pass with an independent re-run (exit 0), security found 0 high and 2 medium findings, and rollback is trivial (no DB, in-memory only). The two medium gaps (no store size cap or rate limit, and chunked requests bypass the body-size limit) are denial-of-service risks. They are acceptable for a local or internal release but not for public exposure.
what_will_happen: The release stage records the new in-memory Spring Boot 3.5.6 (Maven, Java 17 target) URL shortener as releasable. This is 18 added files (+717 lines) with no modified or deleted files. It exposes POST /api/links, GET /{code} (302, no-store) and GET /api/links/{code}. There is no database or migration. Data is lost on restart.
risks: Unbounded memory growth (medium): LinkStore.java:11 has no max size, TTL or rate limit, and POST /api/links is unauthenticated. A client can exhaust the heap.
Body-size limit bypass (medium): SecurityHeadersFilter.java:27 checks only Content-Length. Chunked requests report -1 and are fully buffered, so the 8192-byte cap is not enforced.
All data is ephemeral and lost on restart. A later move to a database will need its own migration plan.
Redirect abuse (open redirect or phishing via the shortener) is mitigated by http/https-only validation but is inherent to the product. There is no auth or abuse controls.
Tests were run on JDK 25 while the build targets release 17. The test log shows deprecation and agent warnings (Mockito self-attach, Unsafe) that may break on future JDKs.
